source: Ormerod & MacGregor (2020) The complementary roles of knowledge and strategy in insight problem-solving (CogSci 42), Experiment 1
finding: A direct new head-to-head of representational change (RCT: chunk tightness) and progress monitoring (CSPT: equation value size) in matchstick algebra. Both matter. Tight-chunk problems were harder (RCT holds), but large number values made them much easier (CSPT holds). Value and chunking did not interact.
numbers: N=121 adults (after exclusions), fully between-subjects, 5 min, one problem each. Solved: low-value loose 23/30 (77%), low-value tight 13/30 (43%; the first-move table lists 11/29 for tight), high-value loose 28/31 (90%), high-value tight 24/31 (77%). Logistic model chi2(3)=21.6 p=.001; Chunking Wald=8.12 p=.004; Value Wald=8.65 p=.003; interaction n.s.
limits: Text and table disagree slightly on the low-value tight cell (13/30 vs 11/29). Student volunteers at open days; one item per cell, so item and condition are confounded. Authors are CSPT proponents.
agent_relevance: Both a knowledge-depth signal and a distance-to-goal cue shape which reframe works. A trigger design should not assume one mechanism: use both (see b28).

source: Ormerod & MacGregor (2020) The complementary roles of knowledge and strategy in insight problem-solving (CogSci 42), Experiment 1, first moves
finding: First-move choice shows the same two forces. People start on loose chunks (RCT), but with large value gaps they pick matches that cut the number difference most, even in tight chunks (CSPT).
numbers: First move on a loose-chunk match: low-value loose 28/30 (93%), low-value tight 22/29 (76%), high-value loose 21/31 (63%), high-value tight 16/31 (52%). Model chi2(3)=15.03 p=.002; Value Wald=8.86 p=.003; Chunking Wald=4.71 p=.030; interaction p=.414.
limits: First move was self-reported on paper at 30 s, not eye-tracked.
agent_relevance: The first idea an agent tries is steered by a progress heuristic. Logging the first move per problem tells you which cue is in charge.

source: Ormerod & MacGregor (2020) The complementary roles of knowledge and strategy in insight problem-solving (CogSci 42), Experiment 2 (tautology problems)
finding: Knowledge scope (RCT) sets difficulty: standard tautologies are hard, reverse tautologies easy. But a large value disparity pulled the hard problem up to the easy level. The two factors interacted.
numbers: N=133 adults. Standard tautology: low value 4/32 (12%), high value 21/34 (62%). Reverse tautology: low 23/32 (72%), high 28/35 (77%). Model chi2(3)=39.30 p<.001; Tautology Wald=19.33 p<.001; Value Wald=11.12 p=.001; interaction Wald=5.26 p=.022.
limits: In the high-value standard tautology item one numeral (LI, 51) is the main source of the gap and also lies on the solution path; the effect may be specific to such items. Not preregistered.
agent_relevance: A cue that happens to point at the right move can wipe out a deep-constraint difficulty. In an agent, a cheap salient gap signal may mask whether a true reframe happened.

source: Ormerod & MacGregor (2020), conclusions
finding: The authors argue prior knowledge sets the conditions of difficulty, while search for the move that looks like most progress finds the solution. They claim constraint relaxation is not needed to explain solving. Proponents of RCT could answer with a model that combines spreading activation and inhibition.
numbers: No new numbers; summarises Experiments 1 and 2 (N=121 and N=133).
quote: the mind's 'response to persistent failure' is not to try to forget what it knows; it is to try to find something better
limits: Argument from behavioural data only; no process tracing. Cannot rule out that relaxation occurs and is simply not required for the cue-driven solutions.
agent_relevance: The disagreement is about solution mechanism, not about whether the default frame causes difficulty. Both camps agree the frame sets difficulty. Triggers should therefore target the search step too, not only the frame.

source: Ormerod & MacGregor (2020) The complementary roles of knowledge and strategy in insight problem-solving (CogSci 42), hidden problem for RCT
finding: Raises a logical gap for RCT: if wrong knowledge is switched off to solve, something must switch it back on, and something must activate the right knowledge. Cites later work (Zhang 2015, Oellinger 2017) as confirming scope and tightness effects.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Argument, not data.
agent_relevance: An agent that drops a constraint should restore it afterward and say so, so later steps stay consistent.

source: Oellinger, Fedor, Brodt & Szathmary (2017) Insight into the ten-penny problem: guiding search by constraints and maximization (Psychological Research 81), solution rates
finding: A hybrid test. Relaxing constraints alone (line hint, intersection hint) did not help much. Adding a search criterion (maximize shared pennies) did. So representation change was necessary but not sufficient.
numbers: N=116 analysed (4 groups of about 30). Solved: control 3/30 (10%), line hint 2/29 (7%), intersection hint 6/28 (21%), maximization hint 21/29 (72%). Maximization vs each other group chi2 14.85 to 26.01, p<.0001, phi .51 to .67. 28% of the maximization group still failed.
limits: Hints at 5 min; one problem. Hints can relax several constraints at once, so the groups are not clean single-factor tests. The authors admit another source of difficulty may remain.
agent_relevance: Direct support for pairing a reframe operator with a progress criterion. A reframe prompt alone behaved like the line hint: no gain.

source: Oellinger, Fedor, Brodt & Szathmary (2017) Insight into the ten-penny problem: guiding search by constraints and maximization (Psychological Research 81), what predicts solving
finding: Solvers varied attempts more and tried the intersection idea earlier. In a logistic model, maximization and variation after the hint predicted solving, not group label.
numbers: 32 solvers, 84 non-solvers. Variation rate .59 (SD .24) vs .43 (SD .24), t(114)=3.10, d=.67. Attempts 8.41 vs 10.93, t(114)=2.74, d=.62. Intersection use before hint: 47% of solvers vs 26% of non-solvers, chi2(1,116)=4.56, p<.05. Logistic model Nagelkerke R2=.61; odds ratio 2.18 (maximization), 3.99 (variation).
limits: Post-hoc predictors; the model with interactions was unstable.
agent_relevance: Measure variation across attempts. Repeating a failed approach is a self-made mental set. A cheap trigger: if the last k attempts share the same strategy label, force a different one.

source: Ash & Wiley (2006) The nature of restructuring in insight: an individual-differences approach (Psychonomic Bull Rev 13, 66-73)
finding: A discriminating moderator test. Working-memory span predicted success when the initial search space was large (many moves), but much less when it was small and the problem isolated restructuring. Read as support for automatic redistribution of activation in restructuring.
numbers: Few-moves group n=61, many-moves group n=54, 6 problems, 240 s each. Regression on number solved: WM span beta=.27 p<.01; WM x problem type interaction delta R2=.046, F(1,111)=5.81 p<.05, beta=.267 p=.018.
limits: The isolation is indirect. Interaction effect is small. Later work (Lv 2015, b09) partly agrees; Chein & Weisberg (b10) contest the special-process reading.
agent_relevance: Search over a large space is where working capacity matters; reframing may be cheaper. For an agent, give more token budget to the search phase and a short fixed budget to the reframe step.

source: Lv (2015) The involvement of working memory and inhibition functions in the different phases of insight problem solving (Memory & Cognition 43, 709-722)
finding: Using oral reports to split each solving episode into an initial search phase and a restructuring phase, the two durations were uncorrelated. Working memory span related to the search phase but not restructuring, in both a verbal and a spatial problem. Inhibition effects on restructuring were inconsistent across the two experiments.
numbers: Exp 1: 87 tested, 79 valid, 64 solved. Exp 2: N=119. Search-phase duration negatively correlated with WM span; restructuring duration had no significant WM correlation; latent inhibition correlated with restructuring in opposite directions in Exp 1 (harmful) and Exp 2 (helpful).
limits: Phase boundaries rely on self-reported impasse. Conflicting inhibition signs signal low reliability.
agent_relevance: Supports a two-stage schema: search first, restructure on impasse. Search and restructuring have separable difficulty.

source: Chein & Weisberg (2014) Working memory and insight in verbal problems: analysis of compound remote associates (Memory & Cognition 42, 67-83)
finding: Individual differences in verbal working memory and attention control explained variation in CRA problem solving, including solutions rated as insightful. The authors read this as evidence against a special-process view (business-as-usual).
numbers: Only the abstract and introduction were read; effect sizes not recorded.
limits: Verbal CRA problems, not spatial or multi-step; abstract-level read only. Opposite conclusion to Ash & Wiley on WM, partly because the task differs.
agent_relevance: On word-association tasks, plain controlled capacity helps. Do not assume a separate insight mechanism is needed for every task type.

source: Graf, Danek, Vaci & Bilalic (2023) Tracing cognitive processes in insight problem solving: GAMs and change point analysis (J. Intelligence 11, 86), sudden vs gradual
finding: Eye tracking on a matchstick problem. Solvers' attention to the key plus sign stayed low and then jumped just before the answer. ANOVA hides this abruptness; GAMs and change-point models find it. So representational change looks sudden at the process level when measured properly.
numbers: N=61 (mean age 22.8). 34% solved without hint; a further 11% solved after the hint. Time split into 10 relative bins; solvers' dwell on the key element jumps in the last bin.
limits: One problem, one lab. The jump is in the final 10% bin, so it may be answer announcement rather than prior restructuring. An earlier eye study placed the shift in the last third.
agent_relevance: A sudden shift can be invisible to linear, windowed monitors. A detector for frame changed should look for jumps, not trends.

source: Graf, Danek, Vaci & Bilalic (2023) Tracing cognitive processes in insight problem solving: GAMs and change point analysis (J. Intelligence 11, 86), hints
finding: Explicit hints changed the dynamics. Non-solvers refocused in a burst, then attention faded. Eventual solvers after the hint moved gradually, not suddenly. So a hint is not the same event as a self-made restructure.
numbers: Same sample N=61; hint at 5 min.
limits: Qualitative description; no effect sizes in the text read.
agent_relevance: A prompt that tells the agent where to look produces a different, less durable pattern than self-discovered reframing. Check that the new frame persists over several steps.

source: Oellinger, Jones & Knoblich (2006) Heuristics and representational change in two-move matchstick arithmetic tasks (Adv. Cogn. Psychol. 2, 239-253), via a search summary
finding: A factorial test of heuristics vs representational change. Representational change had a strong effect on solution rates; heuristics had minimal effect. Authors propose representational change as a necessary condition for useful heuristics.
numbers: N=120 (from the summary only). No cell values read.
limits: The PDF could not be opened (HTTP 403 on core.ac.uk; repository redirect). Numbers unverified.
agent_relevance: Opposite direction to nine-dot and ten-penny. Task type moderates: single-move tasks favour the representation account, multi-step tasks favour progress heuristics.

source: Oellinger, Jones & Knoblich (2014) Dynamics of search, impasse and representational change in the nine-dot problem (Psychol. Research 78, 266-275), via a search summary
finding: Three hint groups removed sources of difficulty step by step. Representational change was reached sooner and solving rose with hints versus control. Authors give a staged account: search first, then representational change, then search again in the larger space.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Only an abstract-level summary; full text not opened.
agent_relevance: A staged model (search, impasse, reframe, search again) is the consensus compromise between the two theories.

source: Nasvytis & Fan (2026) Leveraging speech to identify signatures of insight and transfer in problem solving (arXiv 2605.12970), difficulty order
finding: A large new sample reproduces the Knoblich difficulty order: loose-chunk value changes are easiest, tautology hardest. This strengthens the RCT difficulty ranking.
numbers: N=189 (202 recruited, online, think-aloud), 5 matchstick problems each, 4 min cap, 945 trials. Overall 47.5% correct (449/945). Value-loose-chunk 80.7%, tautology 19.2%; value-tight, hybrid and operator types in between.
limits: Online sample; speech may change solving. Problem set differs from Knoblich 1999.
agent_relevance: The ranking by how deeply baked-in the constraint is has been stable across 25 years and samples.

source: Nasvytis & Fan (2026) Leveraging speech to identify signatures of insight and transfer in problem solving (arXiv 2605.12970), transfer
finding: After a first success, people who meet the same transformation again improve fast. Those who meet a different one each time do not. So a discovered frame transfers only to the same type.
numbers: Same condition accuracy rose from .32 (trial 1) to .75 (trial 5); Different stayed .32 to .39. Trial x group beta=-0.524, p<.001. After first success: 83.7% vs 44.0% correct on later trials; time 89.9 s vs 179.0 s.
limits: First success is used as the marker of restructuring. Accuracy gain is partly learning of a trick, not a general ability.
agent_relevance: Store discovered reframes as named patterns and reuse them on the same task type. Do not expect them to carry across types.

source: Nasvytis & Fan (2026) Leveraging speech to identify signatures of insight and transfer in problem solving (arXiv 2605.12970), speech
finding: People talk more on the trial where they first succeed. They keep talking more and start naming the problem type only when the type repeats. Speech may mark a restructure that becomes accessible to report.
numbers: Speech density rose by 0.057 (p=.0004) in Same and 0.040 (p=.0076) in Different at first success; later rise only in Same (beta=.074, p<.0001).
limits: Correlational; speech density has many causes.
agent_relevance: Naming the pattern in words is a marker of a reusable reframe. An agent can ask itself to label the transformation it just used.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) The Metacognitive Bottleneck: Japanese riddles reveal limits of machine insight and self-evaluation (NazoNazo; arXiv 2509.14704), accuracy
finding: On insight-style riddles requiring representational change, most models stay far below people. Reasoning models do better than non-reasoning ones. GPT-5 falls within the human interval.
numbers: 38 LLMs, 201 riddles, retrieval-free zero-shot. On the 120-item subset: non-reasoning 7.6%, reasoning 17.6%, human mean 52.9% (95% CI 46.6 to 59.2; n=126). Full set: 9.42% vs 19.25%, odds ratio 2.29 (1.99 to 2.64). Parameter count did not predict accuracy; release date did.
limits: Human distribution bimodal (peaks 0 and 20 of 20). No formal model-vs-human tests. Japanese wordplay may disadvantage some models. Items are riddles, not matchstick problems.
agent_relevance: Gap between reasoning-tuned and plain models is roughly 2x in odds. Reasoning budget helps but does not close the gap to people.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) The Metacognitive Bottleneck: Japanese riddles reveal limits of machine insight and self-evaluation (NazoNazo; arXiv 2509.14704), verification failure
finding: Models often write the correct answer in the thought log and then do not endorse it. This is a separate failure from not finding it, and rare in humans by the authors' account.
numbers: Verification failures were 5.23% (Gemini 2.5 Flash Preview) to 39.34% (Grok 4) of incorrect answers; DeepSeek-R1-0528 30.57%; Claude Opus 4 25.00% of wrong answers. Counted when a gold answer appears literally in the thought log before the final answer.
limits: Literal string match; may count incidental mentions. Four models with usable logs. Thought logs may not be faithful.
agent_relevance: Generation is not the only bottleneck; endorsement is. A scaffold should have a checkpoint that compares candidates seen in the trace with the final answer.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) The Metacognitive Bottleneck: Japanese riddles reveal limits of machine insight and self-evaluation (NazoNazo; arXiv 2509.14704), language and false insight
finding: Thinking in English vs Japanese did not reliably change accuracy. The authors also saw confident wrong reinterpretations, like a false Aha.
numbers: Grok-4: Japanese 29.5% vs English 48.8%, p=.0071; Claude Opus 4: 36.7% vs 28.7%, p=.356; Gemini 2.5 Flash: 0/12 vs 22/188, p=.369.
limits: Language choice is not randomised; items differ across languages.
agent_relevance: A wrong but confident reframe is a real failure. Triggers need a verifier, not only a reframer.

source: Ji et al. (2025) MathSticks: a benchmark for visual symbolic compositional reasoning with matchstick puzzles (arXiv 2510.00483), accuracy
finding: Matchstick equation puzzles stay hard for strong vision-language models. Reasoning-tuned versions beat plain ones by a wide margin. Humans are far ahead.
numbers: 14 VLMs; 400-item test set (100 per level). With text: o3 60.00%, Gemini 2.5 Pro 45.25%, Gemini 2.5 Flash 26.50%, o4-mini 24.75%, Seed-1.6-Thinking 21.50%, Claude Sonnet 4 2.25%, GPT-4o 0.00%. Humans (3 adults) 91.72%.
limits: Two-stick moves are 82% of instances, so it is not the single-move Knoblich task. Three human raters. No theory comparison inside.
agent_relevance: Matchstick edits reward search over symbol edits; reasoning budget matters (o3 vs GPT-4o: 60% vs 0%).

source: Ji et al. (2025) MathSticks: a benchmark for visual symbolic compositional reasoning with matchstick puzzles (arXiv 2510.00483), perception vs reasoning
finding: Giving the equation as text lifts accuracy a lot; without it, perception is a second bottleneck. Accuracy falls with difficulty level.
numbers: o3: 60.00% with text vs 38.50% without; levels 1 to 4 with text 73/56/56/55%, without text 69/37/30/18%. Gemini 2.5 Pro 51.7% on one-move text puzzles vs 25.8% pure visual.
limits: Confounds perception with reasoning.
agent_relevance: Fix the representation first (text form) before testing reframe logic. Otherwise a perceptual error looks like fixation.

source: d'Aliberti & Horta Ribeiro (2026) The Illusion of Insight in Reasoning Models (arXiv 2601.00514), spontaneous shifts
finding: Mid-trace Wait, re-evaluate shifts in RL-tuned small models are rare and mostly do not raise accuracy. They do not become more frequent with training. The Aha reading of R1-Zero is not supported.
numbers: GRPO-tuned Qwen2.5 and Llama, 1M+ traces, 3 domains (cryptic crosswords, MATH-500, Rush Hour). Shifts in about 6.31% of traces. Raw accuracy difference shifted minus not shifted: Math -19.78pp; Xword -6.24pp.
limits: Small models (two sizes), GRPO-tuned by the authors. Rush Hour accuracy near zero, so it is uninformative. Shift detection by rubric.
agent_relevance: A self-generated wait is not evidence of insight. Do not use the model's own reframing words as a success signal.

source: d'Aliberti & Horta Ribeiro (2026) The Illusion of Insight in Reasoning Models (arXiv 2601.00514), under high uncertainty
finding: Even when the model is uncertain (top 20% entropy), spontaneous shifts do not reliably help.
numbers: Math high-entropy shifts -7.40pp, low-entropy -22.88pp. Xword high-entropy +0.63pp (n.s.). Entropy-shift odds ratio 0.77 pooled (p=.070); positive in Xwords (2.05) and Rush Hour (1.19), negative in Math (0.58).
limits: Entropy split is a fixed percentile per domain.
agent_relevance: Uncertainty alone does not make a spontaneous reframe good. Spontaneous and prompted reframes behave differently.

source: d'Aliberti & Horta Ribeiro (2026) The Illusion of Insight in Reasoning Models (arXiv 2601.00514), forced reconsideration
finding: An externally added reconsideration cue after a first answer helped, most on Math. This is closest to a trigger test: a second pass with a cue beats leaving the model alone.
numbers: Paired Pass 1 vs Pass 2: Math (N=320,000) 32.21% to 40.62%, +8.41pp, 50,574 wrong-to-right vs 23,500 right-to-wrong. Xword (N=83,200) 9.70% to 10.15%, +0.45pp (5,380 vs 5,004). Rush Hour +0.01pp. Gains larger on high-entropy items.
limits: Same cue for all domains; small models. Pass 2 also adds extra sampling, not only the cue. Gain on puzzle-like tasks is near zero.
agent_relevance: Evidence for externally triggered reframing on math-like tasks, and a warning: on puzzles the gain was tiny. A scaffold trigger should be gated and tested per task type.

source: Haq, Chhaya, Pandey & Bhattacharyya (2025) Is your LLM trapped in a mental set? (arXiv 2501.11833)
finding: Tests mental set on mathematical equivalence problems with Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.1-70B and GPT-4o. In-context examples raise exact-match but do not reduce the number of steps. Chain-of-thought raises step counts, unlike human one-step shortcuts.
numbers: No per-condition numbers were available in the page text read. Three models.
limits: Only the HTML text of the preprint (abstract, results summary) was read; no numeric table recovered. Mental set is only one part of insight theory.
agent_relevance: Few-shot examples do not remove entrenched procedure. Chain of thought makes the shortcut less likely, so the default CoT frame may itself be a set.

source: Webb, Little & Cropper (2016) Insight is not in the problem: investigating insight in problem solving across task types (Front. Psychol. 7:1424)
finding: Insight ratings differ across task types (CRA, classic insight, non-insight). Correct solutions drew stronger insight feelings than incorrect ones. Authors argue problem type matters for how well insight predicts accuracy.
numbers: Three experiments; abstract and introduction read only.
limits: No effect sizes recorded. Supports the task-type moderator theme but is about feeling of insight, not theory discrimination.
agent_relevance: The type of task decides what a signal means. Do not apply one trigger across task families.

source: Cross-source synthesis: which experiments discriminate the two theories
finding: Experiments that separate the theories: (1) distance-to-goal cues like number size (Ormerod 2020, b01-b03): progress monitoring predicts a rise, RCT predicts none; the rise appeared. (2) Chunk tightness and tautology scope: RCT predicts, CSPT does not; both effects appeared. (3) Hint tests (b06, b14): reframe-only hints often fail; reframe plus search criterion works. (4) Working-memory moderators (b08, b09): search yes, restructuring less.
numbers: Synthesis of b01-b09; see Jones 2003 in 04_progress_monitoring_theory/evidence_b.jsonl b07 for the car-park test (N=39; 54% vs 92%).
limits: Each comparison is on small, task-specific effects. The theories are not mutually exclusive; a staged hybrid fits most results.
agent_relevance: Plan for both: keep a reframe operator and a progress/search criterion. Order: search, detect stall, reframe, then search again.

source: Cross-source synthesis: trigger design implications for the agent
finding: (a) Do not rely on spontaneous wait cues (b23). (b) A forced second pass helps on math, little on puzzles (b25). (c) Pair any reframe with a search criterion (b06). (d) Prefer relative stall detection and variation tracking (b07). (e) Add an endorsement check (b19). (f) Log the first-move cue to see whether salient value gaps drive choices (b02).
numbers: No new numbers.
limits: Inference, not tested end to end in a single LLM study.
agent_relevance: These six are candidate trigger rules for the schema. The evidence base for each is moderate; first-hand LLM tests are small-model or benchmark-level.
